intro: Atami maps one tree: the Great Camphor of Kinomiya Shrine, one of Japan's Three Great Camphors and, by the government's own 1988 survey, the second largest tree in the country. Local tradition says circling it once adds a year to your life, and every May 5 the shrine holds a festival built around it. Published alone here because the tree itself is the destination, not because Atami's research is finished.
meta_description: The Great Camphor of Kinomiya Shrine, Atami: one of Japan's Three Great Camphors, ranked the country's second-largest tree, free near Kinomiya Station.
question_meta: Atami's oldest and only mapped tree is the Great Camphor of Kinomiya Shrine, one of Japan's Three Great Camphors, free to visit near Kinomiya Station.
question_answer: Atami's only mapped tree, and its oldest, is the Great Camphor of Kinomiya Shrine (Cinnamomum camphora), a National Natural Monument traditionally said to be about 2000 years old, standing in the grounds of Kinomiya Shrine a five minute walk from Kinomiya Station.
question_context: The tree and the shrine share one founding legend: in 710, a fisherman's net kept catching a wooden idol until it told him in a dream to found a shrine wherever seven great camphors grew together. Local tradition holds that circling this one once adds a year to a visitor's life, and every May 5 the shrine holds the Okusu Festival, with a ceremonial dance composed specifically for the tree. Ranked the second-largest tree in Japan by the Environment Agency's 1988 national giant-tree survey, after a camphor in Kagoshima, and one of the country's 'Three Great Camphors'. Around the Meiji Restoration, loggers made a partial attempt to fell it for timber and the surviving trunk split into two; a 1974 typhoon then snapped five metres off the south trunk, and the break is still capped with sheet metal today. Combined, the two trunks measure 15.65 metres round. Its traditional age of about 2000 years is a legend the shrine itself repeats rather than a scientifically dated figure, and no growth-rate estimate has been published, so the page states the range honestly rather than picking a number. Free to enter, and lit nightly from 17:00 to 23:00.

trees.story:
Circle this camphor once, local tradition says, and you gain a year of life. Kinomiya Shrine's Great Camphor is one of Japan's Three Great Camphors, ranked the second largest tree in the country by the Environment Agency's 1988 giant-tree survey, beaten only by a camphor in Kagoshima. Tradition puts its age at about 2000 years, a figure the shrine itself repeats rather than one any dating has confirmed; no growth-rate estimate exists, so it stays a legend on this page rather than a fact.

The shrine's founding story and the tree's are the same story. In 710, a fisherman's net kept catching a wooden idol, until it told him in a dream to found a shrine wherever seven great camphors grew together. This is meant to be one of them.

It has not had an easy few centuries. Around the Meiji Restoration, loggers made a partial attempt to fell it for timber, and the trunk that survived split into two. A 1974 typhoon snapped the south trunk off five metres up; the break is still capped with sheet metal today. Combined, the two trunks measure 15.65 metres round.

None of it has slowed the crowd. Every May 5 the shrine holds the Okusu Festival, with a ceremonial dance composed specifically for the tree, and the whole site is lit through the evening, 17:00 to 23:00, nightly.
